newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrican Bank likely to drain $1 bln Telkom inflow.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican Bank likely to drain $1 bln Telkom inflow.

text.p: Current economic fundamentals suggest that the Reserve Bank would drain much of the liquidity which would flow into the money market from the recently announced Telkom deal, analysts said on Thursday.

U.S.-based SBC Communications Inc and Telekom Malaysia Bhd signed a deal with the South African government last month that gave them a joint 30 percent stake in the telecommunications utility for $1.26 billion rand.

While $260 million of the amount is expected to be used to retire state debt, $1 billion will be deposited in Telkom's private sector bank account -- a move that would impact directly on the money market.
If allowed to flow into the market, the daily shortage could be reduced by about 4.5 billion rand in a couple of months time against current levels of over eight billion.

But analysts said that given burgeoning private sector credit extension, rampant money supply growth and rising inflation, the Reserve Bank was likely to drain most, if not all, of the proceeds through open market operations.
Consumers' insatiable appetite for credit is one of the main factors which Governor Chris Stals has cited as a reason for the bank's current restrictive monetary policy.
It grew 17.34 percent year-on-year in February, confounding economists' expectations that current high interest rates were finally beginning to bite into consumer spending.

And money supply grew 15.82 percent year-on-year -- well above the central bank's guideline of six to 10 percent -- while consumer inflation, 9.8 percent for February, is expected to peak at around 10 percent over the next two months.

"Those three, particularly credit, suggest to me that the possibility of it all staying in is probably a bit remote at this point in time," John Cruickshank, director of Standard Bank's domestic Treasury, said.

Allowing the shortage to fall in the current environment could send the wrong signal to the market that policy was easing, something the Reserve Bank would be reluctant to indicate at this stage, another senior trader said.
"I would think they will take it all out of the system," he said.

Andre Kok, general manager of the Reserve Bank's money and capital market division, said as the details of when the funds would come into the country were still unknown, the central bank had yet to decide on how to deal with the inflow.
A government spokesman told Reuters that the Telkom deal was expected to be finalised within the next two months. "We should have a clearer picture within the next eight weeks," he said.

Kok said the central bank had held talks with Telkom about the inflow. "But we will manage the liquidity as and when it happens," he said, adding that their decision would depend on market conditions at the time.

An economist also noted that as the dollars which Telkom sold to the central bank would be added to the latter's reserves, Stals could wait for recently announced exchange control relaxations to take effect on July 1.

The easing of controls on individuals, which among others will allow South African resident to hold offshore bank accounts, has prompted speculation of an exodus of capital from the country around that time.
Higher reserves would provide the bank with armour to defend the rand in the event of an exodus of capital from the country, the economist said.

On Tuesday the shortage fell to 8.161 billion rand -- its lowest level in two months -- although Reserve Bank officials said the drop was a result of a seasonal decline in notes and coins in circulation and foreign exchange flows.
